items.title: Do Not Pass Go
items.content:
“Later machines will all be designed by ultraintelligent machines, and who am I to guess what principles they will devise?” – Irving John Good
 When Isidore Jacob Gudak was born to Polish immigrant parents in London on December 9, 1916, few could have envisioned the impact his work would have on the future of computational science. Like many new arrivals to Britain, Gudak’s name was later anglicized for assimilation purposes, and Irving John “Jack” Good’s prodigious talent for mathematics was recognized at an exceptionally early age. Legend has it that by age 9 he had both deduced that the square root of 2 was irrational and found solutions to Pell’s equation—intellectual milestones on his journey to earning a doctorate at Jesus College, Cambridge, in 1941.

 Strong nerd vibes | Virginia Tech Science Magazine 
 In popular culture, Good is probably best known for his provocative 1966 paper , “Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine,” which appeared in the appropriately titled journal Advances in Computers . Here’s the oft-quoted money shot:
 “ Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an ‘intelligence explosion,’ and the intelligence of man would be left far behind. Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. ”
 In the modern era of rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), creating Good’s ultraintelligent machine has morphed into the vigorous and controversial pursuit of recursive self-improvement (RSI) by frontier labs, including Google, SpaceX, newly public Anthropic, and still-private OpenAI. Under RSI, AI models master the art of improving themselves, rapidly leading to the intelligence explosion foreseen by Good six decades ago. Although nobody truly knows what RSI will look like, more than enough contemporary prodigies have expressed extreme alarm at the uncontrolled nature of the experiment humanity has embarked upon to raise concern. A recent article in TechCrunch frames the current discourse:
 “ To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals. 
 To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more. ”

 Escape velocity | Getty 
 Presumably lurking under the “ and more ” umbrella are ultrapowerful weapons envisioned by military enthusiasts in the halls of the Pentagon, for it does not take much in the way of AI expertise to deduce that the winning side in the RSI race will possess tools with vast destructive powers. Among the more benign embodiments that mere human conjecture has credibly pondered is an effective end-run around all known encryption technologies, which smarter people than we fear may result from proving P = NP , which they tell us has something to do with polynomial time and its nondeterministic cousin. (Reimann who?)
 Rumors that RSI has indeed been birthed beyond the public’s view have accelerated to the point where one need not be an insider to have heard confirmatory murmurs from someone who is, and such is the backdrop against which we now ponder the bizarre happenings at Nvidia over the past several weeks. Under the premise that the American government believed it had unlocked the geopolitical equivalent of God mode, what might we expect to see in the way of headlines, and are they consistent with the rash of difficult-to-explain ones the world has been treated to thus far in November? Call us crazy, but…

 Read more

items.title: Everything is Awesome
items.content:
“All I know is just what I read in the papers, and that’s an alibi for my ignorance.” – Will Rogers
 Rarely has the House of Saud been so vulnerable. Under the stewardship of Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), the Kingdom has been propping up one side of an ugly civil war in Yemen with the finest Western weapons oil money can overpay for, backing what legacy media outlets call “the internationally recognized government” operating out of Aden.
 Power is rarely made durable by mere proclamation, and a ragtag group of rebels—headlined by an outfit colloquially known as Houthis and the Blowships—has a decidedly different view of local legitimacy, one that it seems more than capable of backing by force. For reasons that are decades in the making, the outcome of this struggle is seen as existential for MBS, both politically and, well, you know the rest.
 Judging by the alarming-to-Riyadh pace at which Saudi-backed forces are collapsing in the face of the Houthi onslaught, the final battle for Aden is fast approaching, and its outcome will undoubtedly be reported as shocking in hindsight. The clues are there for all those willing to look, and the Blowships have made them difficult to miss by broadening their sights to include high-profile symbols of the MBS era:
 “ On October 14 the Houthis said they had struck Aramco’s headquarters ​in Dhahran, Saudi ⁠Arabia’s main eastern oil city. Three people with knowledge of the matter said that attack caused extensive damage. 
 On November 8, the Houthis said they had hit the Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district. The attack caused visible damage to several floors of the tower. Saudi authorities said the damage came after they ⁠intercepted a ​projectile. 
 A strike on November 19 hit a tower belonging to the Public Investment Fund, ​Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack. Three people familiar with the matter said the strike was caused by a Houthi missile. ”

 Stepped in mud, got new brown shoes | Saudi Press Agency 
 As with most perfect storms, worries have a way of stacking up in quick succession, and the Houthi avalanche comes on the heels of nine months of definitely-not-a-forever-war-just-one-that-never-ends involving the US, Israel, and Iran, which Tehran surely knows MBS enthusiastically supported before he suddenly didn’t. The constipation in the Strait of Hormuz has led to rumors of a Saudi funding crisis, the existence of which has been largely kept secret by a stifling censorship regime. Our friend at the popular Substack PauloMacro speculated that the recent downdraft in gold prices was linked to the House of Saud’s declining fortunes and financial excesses. We suspect he is right:
 “ In the meantime precious metals are getting annihilated, and while everyone points fingers at a tightening Fed or draining liquidity, I think the answer is much simpler — gold holders need cash instead, and urgently so. Which brings us back to my recent obsession around Saudi, its equity market (KSA ETF), its sovereign CDS [credit default swaps], and... it’s [stet] banks… 
 I think the Saudi situation is highly vulnerable here, and shockingly invisible (like everything in the press in that part of the world right now). There is a clear deposit shortage in Saud. ”

 Lost my job, there’s a new opportunity | Getty 
 Meanwhile, in the happy talk halls of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Crown Prince’s proxies have fought off the charge of a fiercely motivated army of do-gooders in the war on carbon. Precious few were even aware that COP31 was actually held this year—let alone in nearby Turkey, which apparently now chooses to identify as Türkiye—but reports from the front indicate its mission seems to be derailing :
 “ The United Nations climate talks broke down on Sunday with no final agreement after long-building tensions paralyzed the negotiations, pitting nations seeking to wind down the era of fossil fuels against those aiming to prolong it. 
 The European Union, as well as many smaller countries vulnerable to climate disasters and rising sea levels, rejected a proposed agreement they said stripped out crucial protections and favored countries that export oil, gas and coal. A group of oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia, had blocked any mention of fossil fuels, the root cause of global warming. 
 It was the first time U.N. climate talks broke down over a final agreement since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009. ”

 It’s awesome to win, and it’s awesome to lose | Getty 
 For European Union (EU) bureaucrats, retaining their steadfast opposition to hydrocarbons at a time when their fiefdoms are in existentially short supply—and bursting at the seams with angry populism as a result—is decidedly on brand. So troubling is the pickle in which the EU finds itself that no less an august body than the US Federal Reserve Board has taken notice. In a FEDS Notes essay published on Friday that echoes what we have been foreshadowing since March , the interest-rate gods modeled the suite of potential outcomes facing the Old Continent this winter:
 “ Against this backdrop, this note considers under what conditions Europe could face gas shortages during the 2026–27 winter. Following the analysis in Rua (2023) of Europe’s energy position ahead of the 2023–24 winter, this note projects EU gas inventories through June 2027, under a Baseline and two adverse scenarios. The projections suggest that Europe can get through an average winter without running out of gas, and through a harsh winter too, albeit with stocks lower than it has tolerated in the past. However, a notable decline in LNG imports would leave storage nearly empty by the spring. ”

 Dip my body in chocolate frostin’ | Getty 
 With broad swaths of buffoonery to choose from, you could be forgiven for missing what future swarm-agent historians will dutifully report as the most important news story of 2026, at least thus far. Just four years after ChatGPT sprung the age of artificial intelligence (AI) on the world, frontier models have gone from being unable to count the number of times the letter “r” appears in “strawberry”—it’s three, for those humans still reading this—to helping mathematicians prove one of the most foundational math hypotheses in history:
 “ The Riemann hypothesis, often considered the most important unsolved problem in mathematics, may be the latest to be conquered by artificial intelligence. 
 On Friday, Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on his personal website saying that he had completed a proof of the hypothesis by collaborating with Claude, the company’s AI system. He did not include a traditional mathematical paper to describe the proof, but instead linked to computer code that he claimed would verify the result. ”

 Have you heard the news? Everyone’s talkin’ | Getty 
 While normies are left to ponder the specific importance of this advance, it is the rate of change in technological progress that matters most. In Ray Kurzweil’s spookily prescient 2005 tome The Singularity Is Near , the futurist observed that the doubling time of technology was shrinking exponentially and made the jarring prediction that soon it would take but a single day. Among the many forecasts that seemed outlandish at the time, Kurzweil posited that AI would surpass human-level intelligence by 2029. On a log chart, we suppose he was close enough.
 We close by emphasizing the often-overlooked subtitle of Kurzweil’s book: When Humans Transcend Biology . In his vision, biological brains would merge with machine intelligence by 2045, ushering in a new epoch that would see human intelligence multiplied “ roughly a millionfold .” We suspect that by 2030, Kurzweil will be viewed as a techno-pessimist.
 Alas, as everyone from Ursula to Warsh to MBS to the Green Chicken knows, there’s no room for pessimism. What, don’tcha know? Everything. Is. Awesome.
 “ ♡ Like” this piece, Dave—or HAL might not open that door.

items.title: The Internet of Gas
items.content:
“Poetry is more a threshold than a path.” – Seamus Heaney
 When Kinder Morgan and its venture partners originally constructed the Rockies Express (REX) pipeline between 2006 and 2009, their goal was to move 1.8 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural gas produced in Colorado and Wyoming. The developers terminated the pipeline near the sleepy, 280-resident Ohio River village of Clarington, where the gas could enter the Texas Eastern Transmission and Dominion Transmission pipelines on its journey to numerous final destinations.
 Just as the project was reaching completion, an unanticipated surge of natural gas production in the Marcellus and Utica shales was taking shape. As the Appalachian region quickly became one of the world’s most prolific producers of the fuel, industry players realized that REX flows could be reversed, providing much-needed egress for a part of the country now drowning in supply. With the opening of the Seneca Lateral in 2014, Appalachian gas began linking up with REX in Clarington and flowing to delivery points in Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois.

 Pipeline map circa 2014 | EIA 
 Among those joining the Clarington party was EQT, which brought its Ohio Valley Connector online in 2016 with 850 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) of Appalachian capacity. Its 400 MMcf/d Clarington Connector is set to become operational any day now, and the company is planning to terminate its 1 Bcf/d POWER Pipeline there in 2030. During a recent earnings call, executives from another eager participant, Antero Midstream, signaled that it too might add to the fast-developing Clarington hub:
 “ Antero Midstream (AM) has a new pipeline on the drawing board. During Thursday’s 3Q26 earnings call, CEO Michael Kennedy said AM wants to build a North-South pipeline from Antero Resources’ West Virginia field north to the Clarington, Ohio, market. Kennedy said AM is ‘scoping it right now’ and spending ‘a little initial capital’ to assess it, and that ‘you’ll probably see us FID that in 2027.’ (FID means final investment decision, the point where a company commits to build.) There was no press release. The news came out in answer to a question from a Goldman Sachs analyst. ”
 Clarington’s journey from a village few had ever heard of to one of the most important nodes in America’s rapidly developing natural gas network is testimony to the sheer scale and pace of one of the most complex energy buildouts ever constructed. The country’s staggering array of trunklines, laterals, and spurs almost magically connects abundant methane brought up from deep underground to the countless machines spread across the economy that burn it to do work. A recent study by S&P Global’s Platts indicates that such midstream momentum is unlikely to abate anytime soon:
 “ Midstream companies have stepped up natural gas pipeline projects in 2026 to connect production to an expected surge in demand from LNG terminals, power generators and data centers. 
 Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, has tracked 46.5 billion cubic feet/day of proposed pipeline projects announced so far in 2026. About 20 Bcf/d of this year’s projects originate in Texas. 
 Announcements have ranged from long-haul Permian Basin egress pipelines to links between Texas and Louisiana’s Gillis hub and laterals to individual data center campuses. ”

 Investment splurge | Platts 
 In the midst of such seemingly spontaneous network formations, one is well-served to step back and laterally ponder the attributes of the end state. What does the US natural gas complex look like in a decade or two? How will the forces of arbitrage dictate what must eventually emerge? Can the US parlay this huge energy advantage into sustained geopolitical leverage by pressing its lead in artificial intelligence (AI)? Let’s put a few predictive stakes in the ground.

items.title: Lame Duck à L’Orange
items.content:
“A tax loophole is something that benefits the other guy. If it benefits you, it is tax reform.” – Russell B. Long
 For all the attention given to the lurid, spy-versus-spy details of Jensen Huang’s targeted removal from the top post at the technology giant he founded, a rather more pedestrian threat to America’s AI dominance has long been obvious in open sources: China can build stuff much faster and cheaper than any major Western nation, including electricity-hungry data centers and the power plants that feed them. While the communist nation may be late to the data center construction game, if recent reporting is any indication, it won’t be long before it accelerates into the global pole position :
 “ China is building data centres at rapid speed across its energy-rich hinterland, as Beijing seeks to turn abundant electricity and cheap land into an advantage in the global race to develop AI. 
 The push is creating vast new computing hubs such as Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, where 89 data centres are built or planned. The AI infrastructure build-out is among the fastest and biggest anywhere in the world… 
 China already has 24 gigawatts of operational data centre computing capacity, more than the rest of Asia combined but less than half the 56GW in the US, according to SemiAnalysis, the chip-focused research firm. A further 50GW is under construction or has been announced. ”

 China speed | SemiAnalysis 
 China’s momentum advantage over the US in this regard looks insurmountable when one considers the absolute drubbing data center developers were handed by voters in the midterm elections held on November 3 rd . In a rout with few parallels in American history, initiatives opposing the construction of the spooky boxes passed handily, while those supporting them were summarily rejected:
 “ Data center opponents emerged among the biggest beneficiaries of Democrats’ sweeping victories in the November midterm elections, as voters across 10 states backed restrictions or rejected proposals to develop data centers in their communities, Reuters reported last week. According to Redbud Consulting tracking, 40 of the 41 data center-related ballot measures sought to restrict their establishment. 
 In a majority of counties where these measures appeared on ballots, voters also shifted toward Democratic candidates in Senate races compared with the 2024 elections. The results could signal growing political pressure on the technology industry, with a Democrat-led Congress potentially pursuing tighter oversight of data center development. ”

 We hear they cause cancer | Getty 
 If voter preferences mattered all that much to US political leaders, the country would not find itself in an empire-ending stalemate with Iran, nor would talk of a possible restart of that war be taken seriously. Based on recent legislative maneuvering in Congress, so too might it be with the nation’s aversion to data centers. During the upcoming lame-duck session, a bill that would vastly overhaul America’s all-constraining energy permitting system stands its best chance of becoming law.
 If it does, not only would a globally relevant boom in new energy development of all forms—oil, gas, wind, solar, and nuclear—break out in the US, but also many left-for-dead data center projects would suddenly become viable. If the pieces fall just right, the Jensen affair will be, at best, the second-most impactful event to rock the AI space in the closing weeks of 2026. Let’s head to Washington to judge the prospects of this transformative legislation becoming law.

 Read more

items.title: Cat-Scratch Fervo
items.content:
“If you rush in and out of the clubhouse, you rush in and out of baseball.” – Pee Wee Reese
 It is hardly controversial to say that the quality of companies coming to market via initial public offerings (IPOs) has degraded over time. Investment bankers and other monied beneficiaries are incentivized to feed a seemingly insatiable demand for risk, even if there are a dozen or more duds for every gee-I-wish-I-could-have-been-allocated-more home run.
 There are many ways to quantify this trend, with the most basic among them probing the simple question of whether an aspiring public company is even turning a profit. A widely circulated study of technology IPOs from the University of Florida provides the hard data for one of those charts that also just feels right:

 The data are all the more damning when one considers the flood of private money available for high-risk enterprises, undercutting what had been the primary driving force for tapping public markets altogether. Given the regulatory, compliance, and spotlight risks that come with being a publicly traded company, why bother to run the gauntlet in the first place?
 Consider Fervo Energy, the upstart enhanced geothermal energy play currently bringing online its first grid-scale power production facility in Beaver County, Utah. Despite just recently launching commercial operations, the company plans to produce more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of geothermal power by 2030. It’s an ambitious growth target, one that—if achieved—would certainly disrupt the clean energy market.
 When Fervo first graced these pages in 2025, it was a privately held enterprise backed by a cadre of blue-chip venture capitalists. With a sold-out book of business, it needed only to call upon disciplined execution. Instead, management took the company public in May, raising more than $2 billion in what its bankers undoubtedly thought was a smashing success. By early October, it had become the subject of a scorching short-seller report by Morpheus Research, and its stock closed nearly 70% below its IPO price last week. On Monday, the company released its third-quarter earnings, causing the stock to soar by more than 25% over Friday’s close.

 A hard bell to resist | Fervo Energy 
 What are we to make of this remarkable roller-coaster ride? Is Fervo the next big thing in energy, set to rewrite the rules of what’s possible in the world of carbon-free electricity generation? Or are the short sellers right in their assessment that the company is little more than an overhyped stock promotion led by a management team willing to bend the truth? A fair assessment can hardly be made at arm’s length, but the alternative energy world will either suffer from or be revolutionized by the consequences either way. Let’s dig into the stakes.

items.title: Attrition Pocket
items.content:
“The two most powerful warriors are patience and time.” – Leo Tolstoy
 In 1983, the Soviet Union began constructing the 4,100-foot-long Southern Bridge in Ukraine’s capital city of Kyiv. Also known locally as the Pivdennyi Bridge, the span opened to road traffic in 1990 and metro service in 1992—years that bookend Ukraine’s declaration of independence in the messy aftermath of the Soviet Union’s collapse. As one of a handful of large bridges crossing the Dnipro River—a majestic expanse that runs the full length of Ukraine from north to south, effectively cutting the country in two—the structure is of outsized importance to military planners on both sides of the war:
 “ Almost everything that comes in from Ukraine’s western partners, from shells and missiles to armoured vehicles and fuel, must eventually cross the river to reach the front in the east. 
 Kyiv sits at the heart of this system. The main rail and road routes from the west converge here, while routes from the left bank fan out towards Chernihiv, Sumy, Poltava and Kharkiv. The capital is therefore both a gateway for Western aid and a rear base for operations to the north and east. ”

 Ties that bind | Mostobud 
 Since the earliest weeks of the war in 2022, hardliners within Russia have at times demanded to know why Moscow declined to destroy these crucial logistical links. Some speculated that the bridges were harder to destroy than many understood, while others lamented Russian President Vladimir Putin’s soft touch in his prosecution of the conflict. A month ago, it became clear that the Kremlin had decided the time was finally ripe for a change in tactics :
 “ Russia struck a bridge linking two sides ​of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv for the second successive day, officials said on Friday, part of an intensifying campaign of air attacks on infrastructure ‌that is upending daily life. 
 An evening drone strike on the closed Southern Bridge was the latest in a series of attacks since Thursday that forced the full or partial suspension of traffic across it and two other bridges spanning the vast Dnipro River. ”

 Cutting the ties | Reuters 
 In the ensuing weeks, continued attacks on a number of Dnipro bridges have been reported in open sources, executed with a combination of advanced drones, powerful missiles, and even bombs dropped from Russian aircraft. Official confirmation of the impact of this escalation is understandably difficult to come by, but judging from the worried commentary emerging from unofficial Ukrainian channels, the complete severing of the major bridges would indeed present a serious challenge for the armies fighting Russia on the eastern front.
 Under the premise that Putin is more cunning and sinister than dovish and tepid, and broadening the framework of analysis from the war in Ukraine to the larger global conflict that includes the war against Iran, we have developed an alternative explanation for why Russia waited so long to split Ukraine in two. If we are right, it foretells an imminent climax to what we have modeled as World War III.

 Read more

items.title: Recycle Bin
items.content:
“To create greater convergence, we need more integration.” – Emmanuel Macron
 The global energy behemoth that is the US natural gas industry continues its relentless growth, making a mockery of pessimistic forecasters. One struggles to properly frame the awesome scale of what is transpiring for a lay audience, but let’s try: In 2026, the US is forecast to grow natural gas production by more than the combined total output of the entire European Union (EU). In 2027, it is anticipated to do so again. Appalachian supply is so abundant that spot prices are running at roughly $1-2 per million BTUs, or $6-12 per barrel of oil on an energy-equivalent basis—less than the daily price swing on Brent crude contracts during these turbulent times.

 Huge bounty | EIA 
 In addition to driving wild improvements in drilling technology, these cutthroat prices are also compelling a wave of industry consolidation. Last week, EQT—a company we expect to profile in November’s Pro Tier deep dive—announced its intent to gobble up one of its pure-play competitors:
 “ EQT’s acquisition of rival producer ​Range Resources this week marks the latest consolidation in the natural gas industry, as producers are scrambling to lock in supply to feed growing ‌demand for liquefied natural gas exports and power demand. 
 Canonsburg, Pennsylvania-based EQT said on Monday it will buy Fort Worth, Texas-based Range Resources in a $13 billion all-stock deal that will create the nation’s biggest gas producer. EQT is the second-largest natural gas producer in the US… 
 The deal underscores how top US gas producers are racing to consolidate ahead of what ⁠they expect will be a step-change in domestic demand, driven by new LNG [liquefied natural gas] export terminals coming online and a buildout of gas-fired power plants to supply electricity-hungry data centers—even as a near-term glut has depressed prices and forced operators to curtail output. ”

 Big business | EQT 
 There is little doubt that gas demand for LNG-exporting magic machines will materialize, and progress on the wave of new terminals being thrown up along the US Gulf Coast can be tracked closely. Whether the electricity-hungry data centers get built is another question, and confidence in the bankability of those future flows was undoubtedly shaken by the rout in artificial intelligence (AI) equities last week.
 One gating factor for fulfilling data center demand is a chronic shortage of the gas-fired power turbines required to convert the fuel into electricity. The major suppliers of these sophisticated contraptions are sold out for years, with some reports stating that new orders placed today won’t be filled until 2030. Even some delivery slots for 2032 are being snapped up. In the grand AI race, time is often more important than money, and without the engines available to burn abundant natural gas supplies, the volumes of shale gas coming online might remain excessive.
 Unless, of course, alternatives can be found to fill the demand gap more quickly. Might old engines do the trick? As it turns out, there are tens of thousands of used aircraft engines on planes and in hangars the world over, and—with varying degrees of effort, time, and money—these workhorses can be repurposed for the task. Let’s head to the airport and learn why flying is about to become even more expensive.

items.title: Gating Functions
items.content:
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history. To the victor belong the spoils, right?” – Donald J. Trump
 In the late summer of 2021, heavy oil production in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt temporarily crashed by 25%. The proximate cause of the decline was the need to divert lighter grades of domestically produced crude to the country’s struggling refineries. Those lighter hydrocarbons would normally have been used as diluents to enable transporting Orinoco’s otherwise solid-like oil sludges to markets near and far. Absent the lights, production of the heavies had to be curtailed.

 Black goo | Bloomberg 
 The root cause of the mini-crisis was the cumulative effect of years of suffocating sanctions levied against Venezuela by successive US administrations that made external sourcing of materials, capital goods, and investor money progressively more difficult. In the final weeks of 2025, such financial weapons were supplemented with floating ones, as the US Navy imposed a partial blockade of oil tankers into and out of the beleaguered country. Among those inbound, a few that of Russian origin found themselves in a particularly interesting showdown :
 “ A tanker subject to US sanctions carrying some 300,000 barrels of naphtha from Russia entered Venezuelan waters late on Thursday, while another began redirecting course in the Atlantic Ocean, ship tracking data showed, a reflection of diverging last-minute decisions by ship owners after President Donald Trump ordered a ‘blockade’ of oil tankers under sanctions bound for the OPEC country earlier this week. 
 The move ramped up pressure on Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro by targeting the country’s main source of income and followed the seizure by the US of an oil tanker off the coast of Venezuela earlier in December. ”
 The naphtha en route from Russia was itself meant to serve as diluent, and Venezuela’s inability to source it in sufficient quantities was once again contributing to precipitously falling production. The escalating pressure campaign that followed culminated in the US Army’s elite Delta Force successfully snatching President Nicolás Maduro in early January, a jarring inflection point in the long-standing geopolitical skirmish between the two countries.

 Heavy stuff | Getty 
 Maduro’s abrupt departure left behind a government that was more pliant to US President Donald Trump’s demands. Much of the sanctions pressure exited with the former strongman, and the flow of diluent in and heavy crude out rebounded markedly. According to a recent report delivered to acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez last week, oil production reached a remarkable 1.25 million barrels per day (bpd)—up from a low of just 830,000 bpd in December—due to higher production in the Orinoco Belt and conventional crude production gains.
 If one closely examines the political and molecular mayhem that has so characterized the Venezuelan oil industry over the past decade, powerful evidence emerges for many of the core themes regularly argued in these pages. Included among them are proof of the shifting molecular definition of oil itself, a proper ranking of politics ahead of geology in the hierarchy of constraints on oil production, and—perhaps most importantly—a window into the true hydrocarbon potential of the Western Hemisphere. Let’s head to Caracas to explore each in order.

 Read more
